title: Closing the Loop: Non-Causal Computation, Partial Traces, & Postselected Entanglement
abstract: This paper gives a categorical interpretation of Baumeler \& Wolf's logically consistent non-causal circuits, connecting them to postselected quantum teleportation. Looped feedback is represented by a trace in the category of non-negative matrices, and it is shown that the traced process is stochastic precisely when the induced loop transition matrix has trace $1$ for every external input, a condition shown to be equivalent to a unique fixed point for the loop for each input to a deterministic circuit. A classical non-causal circuit is represented by a measure-and-prepare quantum channel with an internal register utilising a maximally entangled Bell-state with postselection. The main result is that classical logical consistency is equivalent to the postselected Bell outcome having, for loop dimension $d$, probability exactly $1/d^2$ for each classical input distribution. The subsequent normalised conditional output then agrees exactly with the classical categorical trace. This work identifies a class of quantum Bell-postselection constructions whose conditional evolution maintains linear dependence on classical input distributions.
summary: This paper mathematically interprets non-causal quantum computation using category theory, linking it to postselected quantum teleportation. It proves that the logical consistency of these circuits is equivalent to specific trace conditions on the underlying process matrices. Ultimately, it shows this consistency manifests physically as a uniform probability distribution ($1/d^2$) in the postselected Bell measurement outcomes.
main_problem: The paper aims to provide a rigorous categorical interpretation of non-causal quantum computation models, specifically connecting them to the physical process of postselected quantum teleportation.
main_result: It establishes that classical logical consistency in these non-causal circuits is mathematically equivalent to the postselected Bell outcome having a uniform probability of $1/d^2$ for all classical inputs.
method: The authors employ a categorical framework using traced monoidal categories ($	ext{MatR}^{\ge 0}$) to define and analyze the process's consistency conditions.
model_or_system: The model involves non-causal circuits, which are analyzed via a categorical trace operation ($	ext{Tr}_C(P)$) applied to a stochastic map $P$. This is physically mapped onto a process involving postselection on a maximally entangled Bell state.
key_observables: The stochastic nature of the traced process ($	ext{Tr}_C(P) \in 	ext{Stoch}$), the trace of the induced loop transition matrix ($	ext{tr}(H_a) = 1$), and the probability of the postselected Bell outcome ($1/d^2$).
important_parameters: The loop dimension $d = |C|$, which dictates the required probability $1/d^2$ for classical consistency.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the process $P$ is stochastic for the trace to be well-defined in the context of the category $	ext{Stoch}$.
paper_structure: The paper develops the categorical framework, proves the equivalence between the categorical trace being stochastic and the loop transition matrix having trace 1 (Theorem 1), and then extends this to show the equivalence between this condition and the specific probability distribution arising from postselected Bell measurements (Theorem 3).
why_interesting: The work provides deep mathematical tools (category theory) to analyze the fundamental constraints of causality and information flow in quantum computation, which is highly relevant for understanding resource theories and computational limits.
